item.title: “Monks, a jackal saw a tortoise from afar and approached it. Having approached, it stood to one side and thought: ‘When this tortoise stretches out…
item.description:
“Monks, a jackal saw a tortoise from afar and approached it. Having approached, it stood to one side and thought: ‘When this tortoise stretches out any of its limbs or its neck, I will seize it right there, break it, and eat it.’ But, monks, because the tortoise did not stretch out any limb or its neck, the jackal became disenchanted with the tortoise and left, not having gained an opportunity. So too, monks, Māra constantly and relentlessly stands in ambush for you, thinking: ‘Perhaps I can gain an opportunity through the eye … through the tongue … through the mind.’ Therefore, monks, guard the sense faculties. When you see a form with the eye, do not grasp the general feature, do not grasp the particular feature. Those causes whereby, if the eye faculty were not restrained, covetousness, sorrow, evil, unwholesome states would arise — restrain that cause, guard the eye, practice restraint of the eye. When you hear a sound … smell an odor … taste a flavor … feel a touch … cognize a phenomenon with the mind, do not grasp the general feature, do not grasp the particular feature. Those causes whereby, if the mind faculty were not restrained, covetousness, sorrow, evil, unwholesome states would arise — restrain that cause, guard the mind, practice restraint of the mind. Monks, when you live guarding the sense faculties, Māra will become disenchanted with you and leave, not gaining an opportunity, just like the jackal with the tortoise.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.240

item.title: Elder Añña-Koṇḍañña: I am exceedingly joyful, Having heard the supreme Dhamma, The Dhamma taught for dispassion, Completely without clinging. In this world of a round…
item.description:
Elder Añña-Koṇḍañña:

I am exceedingly joyful,
Having heard the supreme Dhamma,
The Dhamma taught for dispassion,
Completely without clinging.

In this world of a round earth,
With many colors and forms,
Bewildering the mind —
Thus I thought:
The sign of beauty is very enticing,
Connected with lust.

As wind blows away dust,
As rain settles it down,
Thoughts become stilled
When seen with wisdom.

All conditioned things are impermanent —
When seen with wisdom,
One becomes disenchanted with suffering —
This is the path to purity.

All conditioned things are suffering —
When seen with wisdom,
One becomes disenchanted with suffering —
This is the path to purity.

All phenomena are not-self —
When seen with wisdom,
One becomes disenchanted with suffering —
This is the path to purity.

From: Theragāthā 15.1
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: Elder Nun Selā: You will not escape, You will not escape this world. What use is this practice of seclusion to you? Enjoy sensual pleasures…
item.description:
Elder Nun Selā:

You will not escape,
You will not escape this world.
What use is this practice of seclusion to you?
Enjoy sensual pleasures —
Do not have regrets later.

Sensual pleasures are like swords and spears —
They cut the aggregates to pieces.
What you call the pleasure of life —
For me, that sensual pleasure
Is no longer enticing.

Everywhere, delight is destroyed.
The mass of darkness,
The blinding darkness, has been shattered.
Know this, O Evil One —
You are Māra,
You are defeated.

From: Therīgāthā 3.7
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Good is restraint over the eye, Good is restraint over the ear, Good is restraint over the nose, Good is restraint over the tongue.” “Good…
item.description:
“Good is restraint over the eye,
Good is restraint over the ear,
Good is restraint over the nose,
Good is restraint over the tongue.”

“Good is restraint over the body,
Good is restraint over speech,
Good is restraint over the mind,
Good is restraint everywhere.
A monk restrained everywhere
Is freed from all suffering.”

“One who controls his hands and feet,
Controls his speech and his head,
Delights in inner seclusion,
Is content, lives alone —
Him they call a monk.”

From: Dhammapada 360-382

item.title: “And what, Ānanda, is the perception of peril? Here, Ānanda, a monk, going to the forest, to the root of a tree, or to an…
item.description:
“And what, Ānanda, is the perception of peril? Here, Ānanda, a monk, going to the forest, to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, reflects: ‘This body is of much suffering, of much peril. Various diseases arise in this body, such as: eye disease, ear disease, nose disease, tongue disease, body disease, head disease, ear-edge disease, mouth disease, tooth disease, cough, asthma, catarrh, fever, aging, abdominal pain, fainting, dysentery, colic, cholera, leprosy, boils, eczema, tuberculosis, epilepsy, skin disease, itch, scab, ringworm, scabies, blood-bile disorder, diabetes, hemorrhoids, cancer, sores, ulcerations; diseases born of bile, born of phlegm, born of wind, born of the combination of humors; diseases born of change of season, born of improper behavior, born of sudden assault, born of the result of kamma; cold, heat, hunger, thirst, defecation, urination.’ Thus he dwells contemplating peril in this body.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.60
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Mahāli, there is a cause, a condition for the defilement of beings. Mahāli, there is a cause, a condition for the purification of beings.” “But,…
item.description:
“Mahāli, there is a cause, a condition for the defilement of beings. Mahāli, there is a cause, a condition for the purification of beings.” “But, venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the condition for the defilement of beings?” “Mahāli, if form were exclusively suffering, immersed in suffering, accompanied by suffering, not accompanied by happiness, beings would not become lustful for form. But because form is happiness, Mahāli, immersed in happiness, accompanied by happiness, not accompanied by suffering, beings become lustful for form. Through lust, they are bound; through being bound, they are defiled. This, Mahāli, is the cause, this is the condition for the defilement of beings. Such being the cause, such being the condition, beings are defiled.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.60
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: - “Venerable Bharadvāja, what is the cause, what is the reason why these young monks, youthful, with black hair, endowed with the blessing of youth,…
item.description:
- “Venerable Bharadvāja, what is the cause, what is the reason why these young monks, youthful, with black hair, endowed with the blessing of youth, in the prime of life, do not indulge in sensual pleasures and live the perfectly pure holy life for their whole life, completing it fully?” - “Great king, the Blessed One, the Knower, the Seer, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has said: ‘Come, monks, regarding those who are like mothers, establish a mother’s mind. Regarding those who are like sisters, establish a sister’s mind. Regarding those who are like daughters, establish a daughter’s mind.’ This, great king, is the cause, this is the reason why these young monks … live the holy life completely.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.127

item.title: Having abandoned sensual desires in the world, Homeless, gone forth into renunciation, Having abandoned sensual desire and existence, That one I call a true brahmin.…
item.description:
Having abandoned sensual desires in the world,
Homeless, gone forth into renunciation,
Having abandoned sensual desire and existence,
That one I call a true brahmin.

Having abandoned greed and ill-will in the world,
Homeless, gone forth into renunciation,
Having abandoned ill-will and existence,
That one I call a true brahmin.

Who has abandoned the human yoke
And transcended the heavenly yoke,
Having abandoned all yokes,
Released from all bondage —
That one I call a true brahmin.

Having abandoned pleasure and displeasure,
Cooled, without substratum,
A hero who has conquered all worlds,
Mighty and courageous —
That one I call a true brahmin.

Who fully and truly knows
The passing away and rebirth of beings,
Not clinging, well-gone, awakened,
Attained to perfect enlightenment —
That one I call a true brahmin.

Who has no clinging to the past,
The future, or the present,
Not clinging, without possessions —
That one I call a true brahmin.

Who knows his former abodes,
Sees heavenly and evil destinations,
And has attained the destruction of birth —
That one I call a true brahmin.

From: Majjhima Nikāya 98 – Vāseṭṭhasutta
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Truly, brahmins, this world is led by aging, illness, and death. Since the world is led by aging, illness, and death, brahmins, restraint of body,…
item.description:
“Truly, brahmins, this world is led by aging, illness, and death. Since the world is led by aging, illness, and death, brahmins, restraint of body, speech, and mind in this life is a refuge, a cave, an island, a shelter, and a destination for one who has gone to death.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.51
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monk, ‘butcher’s knife’ is a synonym for the five strands of sensual pleasure; ‘lifting the butcher’s knife’ means abandoning these five strands of sensual pleasure.…
item.description:
“Monk, ‘butcher’s knife’ is a synonym for the five strands of sensual pleasure; ‘lifting the butcher’s knife’ means abandoning these five strands of sensual pleasure. ‘The wise man, taking the sword, dug up’ is the meaning. ‘Piece of meat’ is a synonym for delight and lust; ‘lifting the piece of meat’ means abandoning that delight and lust. ‘The wise man, taking the sword, dug up’ is the meaning. ‘Viper’ is a synonym for a monk who has destroyed the defilements; ‘let the viper be, do not touch the viper, pay homage to the viper’ is the meaning.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 23 – Vammikasutta
